In [computer science](/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science"), **declarative programming** is a [programming paradigm](/wiki/Programming_paradigm "Programming paradigm") that expresses the [logic](/wiki/Logic "Logic") of a [computation](/wiki/Computation "Computation") without fully describing its [control flow](/wiki/Control_flow "Control flow").[\[1\]](#cite_note-1)

The paradigm focuses on abstracting a program beyond the order of execution. This implies usage of a [high-level programming language](/wiki/High-level_programming_language "High-level programming language").

Languages that permit this style allow a developer to minimize or eliminate [side effects](/wiki/Side_effect_\(computer_science\) "Side effect (computer science)") by describing *what* the program must accomplish in terms of the [problem domain](/wiki/Domain_knowledge "Domain knowledge"), rather than fully describing *how* to accomplish it as a sequence of the programming [language primitives](/wiki/Language_primitive "Language primitive") (the *how* being left up to the language's [implementation](/wiki/Programming_language_implementation "Programming language implementation")). Declarative programming is in contrast with [imperative programming](/wiki/Imperative_programming "Imperative programming"), which implements [algorithms](/wiki/Algorithm "Algorithm") in explicit steps.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Sebesta_2016-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

Just like in the [functional programming](/wiki/Functional_programming "Functional programming") paradigm, [mutating variables](/wiki/Immutable_object "Immutable object") does not conform to the declarative paradigm because it implies an execution order which is [imperative](/wiki/Imperative_programming "Imperative programming").

Declarative programming may consider [programs](/wiki/Program_\(machine\) "Program (machine)") as [theories](/wiki/Theory_\(mathematical_logic\) "Theory (mathematical logic)") of a [formal logic](/wiki/Mathematical_logic#Formal_logical_systems "Mathematical logic"), and computations as deductions in that logical theory. Declarative programming at times simplifies the writing of [parallel programs](/wiki/Parallel_computing "Parallel computing").[\[4\]](#cite_note-4)

Common declarative language paradigms include [logic programming](/wiki/Logic_programming "Logic programming") (e.g., [Prolog](/wiki/Prolog "Prolog"), [Datalog](/wiki/Datalog "Datalog"), [answer set programming](/wiki/Answer_set_programming "Answer set programming")), and [algebraic modeling](/wiki/Algebraic_modeling_language "Algebraic modeling language") systems.

Some logic programming languages, such as [Prolog](/wiki/Prolog "Prolog"), and [database query languages](/wiki/Query_language "Query language"), such as [SQL](/wiki/SQL "SQL"), while declarative in principle, also support a procedural style of programming.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)

Other definitions:

*   Any programming language that lacks [side effects](/wiki/Side_effect_\(computer_science\) "Side effect (computer science)"), or more specifically, has [referential transparency](/wiki/Referential_transparency "Referential transparency").
*   A language with a clear correspondence to [mathematical logic](/wiki/Mathematical_logic "Mathematical logic").[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)

## Subparadigms

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&veaction=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Subparadigms") | [edit source](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section's source code: Subparadigms")\]

Declarative programming is an [umbrella term](/wiki/Umbrella_term "Umbrella term") that includes a number of better-known [programming paradigms](/wiki/Programming_paradigm "Programming paradigm").

### Functional Programming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&veaction=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Functional Programming") | [edit source](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section's source code: Functional Programming")\]

Further information: [Functional programming](/wiki/Functional_programming "Functional programming")

In a [pure functional language](/wiki/Pure_functional_language "Pure functional language"), such as [Haskell](/wiki/Haskell "Haskell"), all functions are [without side effects](/wiki/Pure_function "Pure function"), and state changes are only represented as functions that transform the state, which is explicitly represented as a [first-class](/wiki/First-class_citizen "First-class citizen") object in the program. Although pure functional languages are non-imperative, they often provide a facility for describing the effect of a function as a series of steps.

### Constraint programming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&veaction=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Constraint programming") | [edit source](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section's source code: Constraint programming")\]

Further information: [Constraint programming](/wiki/Constraint_programming "Constraint programming")

Constraint programming states relations between [variables](/wiki/Variable_\(high-level_programming_language\) "Variable (high-level programming language)") in the form of constraints that specify the properties of the target solution. The set of constraints is [solved](/wiki/Solver_\(computer_science\) "Solver (computer science)") by giving a [value](/wiki/Value_\(computer_science\) "Value (computer science)") to each variable so that the solution is consistent with the maximum number of constraints. Constraint programming often complements other paradigms: functional, logical, or even imperative programming.

### Hybrid languages

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&veaction=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Hybrid languages") | [edit source](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section's source code: Hybrid languages")\]

See also: [Multi-paradigm programming language](/wiki/Multi-paradigm_programming_language "Multi-paradigm programming language")

Makefiles, for example, specify dependencies in a declarative fashion,[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) but include an imperative list of actions to take as well. Similarly, yacc specifies a context free grammar declaratively, but includes code snippets from a host language, which is usually imperative (such as [C](/wiki/C_\(programming_language\) "C (programming language)")).

### Logic programming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&veaction=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Logic programming") | [edit source](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section's source code: Logic programming")\]

Further information: [Logic programming](/wiki/Logic_programming "Logic programming")

Logic programming languages are characterized by a mostly declarative programming style. In logic programming, programs consist of sentences expressed in [logical form](/wiki/Logical_form "Logical form"), and computation uses those sentences to solve problems, which are also expressed in logical form.

Logic programming languages, such as [Prolog](/wiki/Prolog "Prolog"), [Datalog](/wiki/Datalog "Datalog") and [answer set programming](/wiki/Answer_set_programming "Answer set programming"), compute by proving that a goal is a logical consequence of the program, or by showing that the goal is true in a model defined by the program. Prolog computes by reducing goals to subgoals, top-down using [backward reasoning](/wiki/Backward_chaining "Backward chaining"), whereas most Datalog systems compute bottom-up using [forward reasoning](/wiki/Forward_chaining "Forward chaining"). Answer set programs typically use [SAT solvers](/wiki/Boolean_SAT_solver "Boolean SAT solver") to generate a model of the program.

### Modeling

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&veaction=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Modeling") | [edit source](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section's source code: Modeling")\]

Further information: [Mathematical model](/wiki/Mathematical_model "Mathematical model")

Models, or mathematical representations, of physical systems may be implemented in computer code that is declarative. The code contains a number of equations, not imperative assignments, that describe ("declare") the behavioral relationships. When a model is expressed in this formalism, a computer is able to perform algebraic manipulations to best formulate the solution algorithm. The mathematical causality is typically imposed at the boundaries of the physical system, while the behavioral description of the system itself is declarative or acausal. Declarative [modeling languages](/wiki/Modeling_language "Modeling language") and environments include [Analytica](/wiki/Analytica_\(software\) "Analytica (software)"), [Modelica](/wiki/Modelica "Modelica") and [Simile](/w/index.php?title=Simile_\(computing\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Simile (computing) (page does not exist)").[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)

## Examples

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&veaction=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Examples") | [edit source](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section's source code: Examples")\]

### Prolog

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&veaction=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Prolog") | [edit source](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section's source code: Prolog")\]

[Prolog](/wiki/Prolog "Prolog") (1972) stands for "PROgramming in LOGic." It was developed for natural language [question answering](/wiki/Question_answering "Question answering"),[\[9\]](#cite_note-PrologHistory-9) using SL resolution[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) both to deduce answers to queries and to parse and generate natural language sentences.

The building blocks of a Prolog program are *facts* and *rules*. Here is a simple example:

cat(tom).                        % tom is a cat
mouse(jerry).                    % jerry is a mouse

animal(X) :- cat(X).             % each cat is an animal
animal(X) :- mouse(X).           % each mouse is an animal

big(X)   :- cat(X).              % each cat is big
small(X) :- mouse(X).            % each mouse is small

eat(X,Y) :- mouse(X), cheese(Y). % each mouse eats each cheese
eat(X,Y) :- big(X),   small(Y).  % each big being eats each small being

Given this program, the query `eat(tom,jerry)` succeeds, while `eat(jerry,tom)` fails. Moreover, the query `eat(X,jerry)` succeeds with the answer substitution `X=tom`.

Prolog executes programs top-down, using [SLD resolution](/wiki/SLD_resolution "SLD resolution") to [reason backwards](/wiki/Backward_chaining "Backward chaining"), reducing goals to subgoals. In this example, it uses the last rule of the program to reduce the goal of answering the query `eat(X,jerry)` to the subgoals of first finding an X such that `big(X)` holds and then of showing that `small(jerry)` holds. It repeatedly uses rules to further reduce subgoals to other subgoals, until it eventually succeeds in [unifying](/wiki/Unification_\(computer_science\)#Application:_unification_in_logic_programming "Unification (computer science)") all subgoals with facts in the program. This backward reasoning, goal-reduction strategy treats rules in logic programs as procedures, and makes Prolog both a declarative and [procedural programming](/wiki/Procedural_programming#Logic_programming "Procedural programming") language.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11)

The broad range of Prolog applications is highlighted in the Year of Prolog Book,[\[12\]](#cite_note-Prolog_Book-12) celebrating the 50 year anniversary of Prolog.

### Datalog

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&veaction=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Datalog") | [edit source](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section's source code: Datalog")\]

The [origins of Datalog](/wiki/Datalog#History "Datalog") date back to the beginning of logic programming, but it was identified as a separate area around 1977. [Syntactically and semantically](/wiki/Syntax_and_semantics_of_logic_programming "Syntax and semantics of logic programming"), it is a subset of Prolog. But because it lacks [compound terms](/wiki/Prolog#Data_types "Prolog"), it is not [Turing-complete](/wiki/Turing_completeness "Turing completeness").\[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*\]

Most Datalog systems execute programs bottom-up, using rules to [reason forwards](/wiki/Forward_chaining "Forward chaining"), deriving new facts from existing facts, and terminating when there are no new facts that can be derived, or when the derived facts unify with the query.\[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*\]

Datalog has been applied to such problems as [data integration](/wiki/Data_integration "Data integration"), [information extraction](/wiki/Information_extraction "Information extraction"), [networking](/wiki/Computer_network "Computer network"), [security](/wiki/Security "Security"), [cloud computing](/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing") and [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning").[\[13\]](#cite_note-13)[\[14\]](#cite_note-14)

### Answer set programming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&veaction=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Answer set programming") | [edit source](/w/index.php?title=Declarative_programming&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section's source code: Answer set programming")\]

[Answer set programming](/wiki/Answer_set_programming "Answer set programming") (ASP) evolved in the late 1990s, based on the [stable model](/wiki/Stable_model_semantics "Stable model semantics") (answer set) semantics of logic programming. Like Datalog, it is a subset of Prolog; and, because it lacks compound terms, it is not Turing-complete.

Most implementations of ASP execute a program by first *grounding* the program, replacing all variables in rules by constants in all possible ways, and then using a propositional SAT solver, such as the [DPLL algorithm](/wiki/DPLL_algorithm "DPLL algorithm") to generate one or more models of the program.

Its applications are oriented towards solving difficult [search problems](/wiki/Search_algorithm "Search algorithm") and [knowledge representation](/wiki/Knowledge_representation "Knowledge representation").[\[15\]](#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)
